newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour steal Conservatives' tax clothes.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour steal Conservatives' tax clothes.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party offered on Monday the hardest evidence yet that it has cast off its reputation for economic irresponsibility by matching the government's pledge to keep taxes and spending down.

In the first of a series of speeches detailing his policies, economics spokesman Gordon Brown said a Labour government would not raise the basic rate of tax for the five-year life of the next parliament or increase spending for at least two years.
Conservative ministers, who intend to fight the coming election on a record of sound economic management, were wrong-footed by the announcement and dismissed it as incredible.
Brown, however, said Labour, in opposition since 1979 but far ahead in opinion polls, was deadly serious: "We are wise spenders, not big spenders."
Political commentators said the impact of Brown's pledge could be decisive at the coming election, which Prime Minister John Major must hold by May 22.

"In the long run-up to the general election, Mr Brown's remarks this morning could prove, with hindsight, to have provided the knock-out blow to Mr Major," London's Evening Standard newspaper commented in an editorial.

Labour's unexpected defeat in the 1992 election was widely blamed on its economic policies. Voters feared they would have to pay more tax to pay for the party's ambitious spending plans and kept faith with the Conservatives despite a deep recession.
Brown acknowledged that a myth had grown up in the Labour Party that every problem could be solved by spending more.
Such an approach was not only imprudent, it had become impossible because of the global economy. Financial markets, he said, would swiftly punish irresponsible tax-and-spend policies.
"So we reject the old Labour litmus test on spending: that increasing the overall level of spending is proof of our socialist commitment," Brown said.

"While government still has and must have a clear responsibility to advance the public interest, we do not make the mistake of equating this with a commitment to inexorable increases in public spending," he added.

His words testifed to the transformation of Labour under moderate leader Tony Blair. A party once committed to public ownership of the "commanding heights of the economy" is now discussing how to run capitalism more humanely.

At a hastily arranged news conference, Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke said no one would believe Brown's promises in light of Labour's record of opposing government measures to rein in spending.
He said Labour had already made pledges involving some 30 billion pounds ($50 billion) of extra public spending.
"Gordon Brown's claim that he could control public spending is beyond belief," Clarke said. "Hell will freeze before Gordon Brown could control spending and keep tax down."

Brown had been expected to rule out a rise in the top rate of income tax, currently 40 percent. But he went much further, promising no increase in either top-rate tax or the 23 percent basic tax rate during the five years of the next parliament.
He also risked the wrath of Labour left-wingers and trade unions by promising to extend a four-year-old pay freeze for Britain's six million public sector workers.

Major favours a May 1 election but after the death of a Conservative MP pushed his government into a minority position in parliament last week, there was speculation he might be forced into an earlier poll.
On Monday, Labour said one of its MPs, Martin Redmond, has also died, meaning the 322 Conservative MPs are now faced by the same number of legislators from opposition parties.
